entry.title: SLM-default, LLM-fallback pattern with Agent Framework and Azure AI Foundry
entry.summary: When building AI workflows, we often face a choice: do we use a massive, expensive cloud model for everything (to ensure best reasoning capabilities), or do we cut costs with a smaller local model (and risk hallucinations)? In this post, we’ll explore a “best of both worlds” architecture, as described in the recent survey “Small Language Models for Agentic Systems” Sharma & Mehta, 2025. We call this the “SLM-default, LLM-fallback” pattern. The premise is simple: route all queries to a fast, private, on-device Small Language Model (SLM) first. Only if that model cannot confidently answer the query, do we escalate the request to a paid cloud model (LLM).

entry.title: Don’t Drop the Data: Engineering a Robust Soft Delete Pattern in EF Core
entry.summary: Soft delete is one of the most enduring patterns in enterprise systems: instead of permanently removing rows from your database, you mark them as deleted. This preserves history, enables audits, supports undo operations, and keeps your system safe from accidental “delete catastrophes.” In this deep dive, we implement a maintainable soft-delete architecture using EF Core, global query filters, and a clean, generic repository.

entry.title: SQL Server 2025 Compression Deep Dive: Internals, Performance Gains & Real-World Benchmarks
entry.summary: SQL Server 2025 introduces new observability tools, improved TempDB I/O governance, hybrid buffer pool enhancements, and smarter columnstore metadata. All these changes amplify the benefits of row, page, and columnstore compression. This in-depth technical guide explains how data compression works in SQL Server 2025, what has changed, and includes full hands-on T-SQL examples, test scripts, and best practices for DBAs and developers.

entry.title: dotnet-script 2.0 is out with .NET 10.0 support
entry.summary: Last week, we released version 2.0 of dotnet-script. The latest release introduces support for .NET 10.0 and C# 14 and is available, as usually, through Github releases and on Nuget. You will need to have at least the .NET SDK 10.0.100 installed. It is the first major release of dotnet-script since version 1.0, which was released back in 2020. At the same time, the breaking changes are minimal, and the revision is mostly driven by the careful application of semantic versioning principles.
